newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya shilling stable in 1996, uncertain in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Kenya shilling stable in 1996, uncertain in 1997.

text.p: A less panicky market and increased dollar inflows contributed to a stronger shilling in calendar year 1996 but uncertainty looms in the coming year, commercial bank dealers said on Wednesday.
Major market players said the shilling would close the year around the level of 55 to the dollar but they expressed concern about the shilling's stability with elections due in 1997.

"That's a million dollar question. People get very uneasy around election time, and most investors especially foreigners might walk out," said a dealer, referring to presidential and parliamentary elections due some time next year.
"This year has seen a more stable shilling moving in small margins, unlike last year when the shilling was very volatile," a dealer at a leading commercial bank said.
"In fact, the number of forward deals have improved by about 30 percent mainly due to a stable environment," he added.

The Central Bank of Kenya said in its monthly report for December that the shilling's strength was a reflection of the stable underlying economic conditions that have prevailed from the beginning of the year.
Against the pound, the shilling lost ground in the year, reflecting the weakening of the dollar against the pound in the international market.

Dealers said there was good demand from the traditional importers in the market, mainly oil and motor industry and sometimes from the central bank but this was outstripped by inflows coming in from the agricultural sectors.

"This year, we have seen more orders from foreign investors coming in to buy treasury bills which has also contributed to a stronger shilling -- unlike other years when inflows were mainly from the agriculture (sector)," one dealer added.
Interest offered on government treasury bills has been on a downward trend since October. Rates hovered in the 21 percent region on the main body of 91-day treasury bills.
Financial analysts said that even at that rate, the treasury bill market was still attractive because of the interest rate differentials between the shilling and the dollar.

"Considering the real U.S. interest rate is about 3.0 percent while Kenya's stands at about 10 percent, foreign investors stand to gain with an interest rate differential of about 7.0 percent after inflation adjustment," one said.

The shilling opened January 1996 at an average rate of 55.79 against the dollar amid predictions of stability but quickly dipped to 59.45 by end-month mainly due to speculation in the interbank market focusing on prospects for external finance.
"This led to exporters holding onto their foreign exchange earnings and importers buying spot to cover future foreign exchange requirements," the central bank said in March.
The shilling picked up as market confidence increased following a successful Paris donor Consultative Group meeting.
It maintained its stable tone as the market received higher than expected inflows of foreign exchange and in the absence of market destabilising factors.

In the second half of the year, the shilling broke the 57 level barrier against the dollar, as exporters offloaded heavily in the market. "The market saw importer demand dwindle to a trickle, and a lot of support from the central bank at the 56 level," a dealer said.
